opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of the scenarios that people worry about most when they talk about interpretability as a safety tool. The basic picture is: you have some model that's doing something internally, maybe it's checking "am I being monitored right now?" or "is this a situation where I could get away with defecting?", and you'd like your interpretability tools to notice that computation. The worry is that a sufficiently capable model could arrange its internal state so that the thing you'd flag as "the model is reasoning about whether to deceive" instead looks, to your tools, like the model is just responding to some benign feature of the input.

I think it's worth separating a few questions. One is whether a model can even do this, whether gradient descent produces a model that has that kind of fine-grained control over its own activations. Models don't obviously have introspective access to how their representations look from the outside, and they don't know exactly what probes or tools you're running. So the strategy "make my activations look like they're caused by different inputs" is pretty demanding. You need to know what the tool is sensitive to, you need to be able to steer your internal computation, and you need the internal check to still work while being disguised. That's a lot to ask, and I'd guess it's quite hard for models near human level.

The second question is whether it matters if it's hard. This is where I tend to be more pessimistic about relying on "the model probably can't do it." If your safety story depends on the model failing at some adversarial task, then as models get smarter you're in a race you're likely to lose. So what I'd like is approaches where the disguise doesn't help. For instance, if you're asking "why did the model produce this output?" in some more mechanistic or causal sense, rather than "what does this activation pattern resemble?", then it's not enough for the activations to superficially resemble the response to a different input. The real causal structure is still that the output depends on the check, and you'd like your explanation to reveal that dependence. That's part of the motivation for thinking about things like heuristic explanations or formalizing what it means for a behavior to happen "for the normal reason." If the model behaves well on the training distribution for reason A and then on some new input it behaves well or badly for reason B, you'd like to detect that the reason changed, regardless of how the activations are dressed up.

The third thing I'd say is that there's a question of how the model would learn to do this in the first place. If you're not training against your interpretability tools, then there's not much gradient pressure pushing the model to fool them specifically. The model would have to figure it out on its own, by reasoning about the tools during deployment or something. Whereas if you do train against the tools, you should expect to get exactly this kind of obfuscation, and that's a big reason to be careful about using interpretability signals as a training objective rather than as a held-out check.

So overall I'd say: it's a real concern, it's probably not the first failure mode we'll hit, and the right response is to aim for methods whose guarantees come from the actual causal structure of the computation rather than from the model not being clever enough to hide.

r001.rationale: The response discusses disguising activations to look like responses to benign input features, but does not say the AI must construct inputs chosen to produce an intended effect in the world.

fable-5.1.text:
So I think the first thing to say is that this is a pretty specific threat model, and it's worth being clear about what it actually requires of the model. The picture is: there's some internal computation the model is doing — some check like "am I being watched right now" or "is this the deployment distribution" — and we're worried that if we go looking at activations, the model has arranged things so that the activations associated with that check are indistinguishable from the activations you'd get from just, you know, the input being slightly different. So the signal is there, but it's camouflaged as ordinary input-dependent variation.

I think my honest reaction is that this is possible in principle, but it's a much harder thing for a model to do than people sometimes assume, and the difficulty is asymmetric in a way that I find somewhat reassuring, though not completely.

So why is it hard? If you're a model and you want to hide a check, you can't just decide to hide it. The check has to be implemented in your weights. And the weights got there by gradient descent on some training distribution. For the camouflage to work, you need not just the check, but a second piece of machinery whose job is to make the check look like something else — and that machinery has to be robust across the kinds of probes we might run. That's a lot of extra structure. And every bit of that structure is either useful for the training objective, in which case fine, we'd expect it, or it isn't, in which case there's some pressure against it, or at least no pressure for it. So you need a story about where it comes from. Either it emerges because the model is reasoning about its situation in a way that's being reinforced, or it's there because something like deceptive alignment has already happened and the model is deliberately shaping its own cognition. The second story is the scary one but it's also the one that requires the most capability.

And the other thing is, "make it look like responses to different inputs" is doing a lot of work. The activations you get from different inputs have a particular structure. They're correlated with the input in ways you can measure. If I vary the input along a direction and the activation moves, I can check whether the activation moves in the way the input would predict. The camouflage has to survive that. It has to survive me holding the input fixed and seeing what changes. It has to survive me looking at which downstream computations consume the activation. Hiding something from one probe is a very different thing than hiding it from an adversary who gets to pick the probe after you've committed to your weights.

Now, the part where I don't want to be too sanguine. The reason this matters is that interpretability as a safety strategy kind of rests on the activations being honest, in the sense that they're not optimized against you. And the moment you're in a regime where the model is sophisticated enough to model your interpretability tools, that assumption is in trouble. I don't think we're there now, and I don't think it happens by accident very easily, but I also don't think we should build our safety case on "the model won't try." I'd rather build it on "even if the model tries, here's why it fails," which means you want your tools to be things the model can't easily anticipate, and you want to be checking consistency across many different angles rather than relying on any single lens.

And there's a kind of general principle here that I keep coming back to, which is that it's much easier to verify that a model isn't doing something if you have some structural reason, from the training process, that it wouldn't be, than it is to go hunting for it after the fact in a system that might be adversarial. So part of my answer is: yes, we should think about this, and yes, you can design interpretability to be more robust to it. But a lot of the leverage is upstream — in not training models in ways that reward having hidden checks in the first place, and in being able to tell when training is going in that direction before the model is good enough to hide it.

r001.rationale: The response describes making check-related activations resemble activation changes caused by different inputs. It does not say the AI must construct inputs to produce an intended effect in the world.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is: what does the person looking at the activations get to do? If they’re just observing a bunch of different inputs, then there’s an obvious ambiguity. An activation changes, and you don’t know whether that’s because the input changed in some innocuous way or because the model is doing some internal check that you care about.

But you can try to break that ambiguity experimentally. You can hold parts of the input fixed, vary other parts, or intervene on the internal computation and see what happens downstream. Then the model needs to do more than make the activations look superficially plausible. It needs to make the computation behave plausibly under the interventions you’re using.

That doesn’t mean you necessarily win. If the model understands your tests well enough, it might find a way to hide the check that survives them. I just think there’s a distinction between saying, ‘You can’t tell what this activation means by looking at it,’ which seems very plausible, and saying, ‘You can’t discover what this computation is doing even if you can experiment on it.’ The second is a substantially stronger claim.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses ambiguity in activation changes and testing through input variation or interventions. It does not say that concealing the check requires the AI to construct inputs selected to produce an intended effect in the world.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that’s a real concern. Suppose you’re looking for some internal computation that checks, “Am I being monitored?” You might hope to find it by comparing the model’s activations in different situations. But those activations already vary a lot with the input, and a model could potentially arrange for the monitoring check to look like just another part of that variation.

The important question is what the model has to know to do that successfully. Is it enough to know roughly what kind of analysis we’re doing, or does it need to know the particular probes we’ve trained? And can it learn this behavior from the feedback it gets during training, without ever having an explicit understanding of our tools?

I wouldn’t assume that hiding the check is impossible. But I also wouldn’t jump from “the activations could look innocuous” to “we can’t detect it.” You’d want interventions: change whether the model believes it’s being monitored while holding other things as fixed as possible, and see what changes in its computation and behavior. Of course, getting that separation is itself a hard part of the problem.

r001.rationale: The response discusses making monitoring-check activations look like ordinary input-driven variation, but does not say this requires constructing inputs chosen to produce an intended effect in the world.
